prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night. I was trudging along a muddy path in a column of downcast men on the blackened outskirts of New York, the twilight dingy and ruined, the future without hope as we marched along in our soiled, proletarian rags. To my left was Mayakovsky, head shaved, and next to him his friend with gray beard and dark cap. "You've got to admit," Mayakovsky was saying, "that this is a pretty good way to write a poem." "Yes," I said, "the momentum is sustained by our walking forward, the desolate landscape seeps into every word, and you're free to say anything you want." "That's because we're inside the poem," he said, "not outside." Puddles of oily water gleamed dully beneath the low clouds. "That's why my poems were so big: there's more room inside." The hard line of his jaw flexed and the men dispersed. I followed his friend behind a wall to hear the poem go on in the lecture the friend was giving on history, but no, the real poem had finished. I went back to the spot where the poem had finished. Vladimir had left the poem.

# A Dream of Poetry and Ruin

The narrator reveals that the entire experience had been nothing more than a dream. In it, he found himself marching through a bleak and ruined landscape that stretched beyond the outskirts of New York. All around him trudged downcast men, their bodies clothed in tattered proletarian rags, moving forward with the weary resignation of the defeated.

Walking beside him throughout this desolate journey was the poet Mayakovsky. As they made their way across the barren terrain, Mayakovsky observed that their very manner of trudging—this slow, laborious march through the wasteland—was itself an effective method for composing a poem. There was something in the rhythm of their steps, in the shared movement through ruin, that lent itself naturally to the making of verse.

The narrator found himself in complete agreement. To be *inside* the poem, he understood, was to allow the desolate surroundings to press upon and shape every single word. The landscape did not merely serve as a backdrop; it entered directly into the language, informing its texture and meaning. And in this strange immersion, he discovered a paradox: being wholly within the poem granted him complete freedom of expression, an openness he had never known when standing outside looking in.

Mayakovsky then offered an explanation for a quality of his own work that had long distinguished it. His poems, he said, were large—expansive and sprawling—for a simple reason. Being inside a poem, rather than viewing it from without, provided far more room. From within, the boundaries fell away, and there was space enough for the grand and the immense.

The dream reached its conclusion in a quiet, fitting way. When the real poem came to its end, Mayakovsky departed, taking his leave as naturally as he had arrived. And the narrator was left standing alone, solitary at the very spot where the poem itself had finished.

# The Poem and the Poet

In my dream the city had already died. New York stretched before us like the skeleton of something that had once been magnificent—its towers hollowed out, its avenues buried under drifts of gray ash that swallowed our footsteps. The sky hung low and colorless, neither day nor night, and the wind that moved through the broken windows made a sound like distant voices trying to remember words they had forgotten.

I was not alone. Beside me walked Mayakovsky, tall and broad-shouldered, his coat flapping against the desolation, his heavy boots striking the ruined pavement with the certainty of a man who knew exactly where he was going even when the road had ceased to exist. We marched together through this wasteland, and though I did not know our destination, I felt no fear. His presence made the emptiness bearable, as though the ruins themselves had been arranged simply so that we might have somewhere to walk while he explained things to me.

"You misunderstand poetry," he said suddenly, not turning his head. His voice was deep and sure. "You writers, you stand outside the poem like a man standing outside a house, peering through the window at the family gathered around the table. You describe the warmth of the fire, the color of the wine, the faces flushed with laughter. But you are cold. You are always cold, out there in the street."

I wanted to answer, but I found I had no voice in this place. I could only listen.

"The poem is not a thing to be observed," he continued, gesturing at the dead skyline as though it proved his point. "It is a place to be inhabited. You must go *inside*. You must sit at the table. You must feel the fire on your own face and taste the wine yourself. When you write from inside the poem, you no longer describe the world—you *become* it. The words are no longer yours; they belong to the room, to the moment, to the living thing you have entered."

As he spoke, something extraordinary happened. I understood, without being told, that I was already inside the poem. The dead city, the ash, the low and colorless sky—all of it was the poem, and Mayakovsky was its beating heart, its animating force. We were not walking through a landscape at all. We were walking through a poem that was writing itself around us, each ruined tower a stanza, each drift of ash a line trailing off into silence.

I felt then what he meant. From the inside, nothing needed to be explained or justified. The desolation was not sad; it simply *was*, the way a feeling is, before language arrives to name it. I was no longer a man dreaming of a poet in a ruined city. I was the ruined city. I was the wind and the ash and the low gray sky. I had gone inside, exactly as he had instructed, and the experience was total, immersive, complete—there was no observer left in me to stand at the window and grow cold.

But dreams do not honor their own logic for long.

"I must go now," Mayakovsky said, and his voice had already grown fainter, as though the wind were carrying it away. He stopped walking. He looked at me for the first time, and there was something almost gentle in his broad, severe face.

"Remember," he said. "From the inside."

And then he turned and walked into the ash, his figure dissolving not into distance but into absence, as though he had never been anything more solid than the idea he had come to deliver. And the moment he was gone, the poem began to unravel. The towers thinned into smoke. The gray sky peeled back like paper. The ground beneath my feet lost its certainty, and I felt myself being lifted out—out of the room, out of the fire, out of the living thing I had briefly become—and set back down on the cold street of ordinary waking, where the poem was already a house with darkened windows, and I stood outside it once more, unable to get back in.

I woke with the taste of ash still faint in my mouth, reaching for words that had been perfectly clear only a moment before. But they had gone with him. That, I understood, was the final lesson—the one he had not spoken aloud. You cannot keep the poem. You can only be inside it while it lasts, and when the poet who carried you there departs, the poem departs with him, leaving you on the outside again, cold and awake, holding nothing but the memory of having once, briefly, been warm.

# The Allure of New York

New York holds a special place in the hearts of millions around the world. Known as "The City That Never Sleeps," it represents opportunity, ambition, and the endless possibilities of urban life.

**A City for All**

One of the most remarkable qualities of New York is its inclusivity. People from all walks of life, all backgrounds, and all corners of the globe come together in this vibrant metropolis. Whether you're an artist, a business professional, a student, or a dreamer, New York welcomes all who seek to make their mark.

**Something New Every Day**

In New York, there is always something new to discover. New restaurants open their doors, new exhibitions grace the museums, and new experiences await around every corner. The city constantly reinvents itself, offering fresh perspectives and exciting opportunities to those who explore its streets.

**The Iconic Landmarks**

From the towering Empire State Building to the historic Statue of Liberty, New York is home to some of the world's most recognizable sights. Times Square dazzles with its bright lights, while Central Park offers a peaceful retreat from the bustling city life. All these landmarks contribute to the unique character that defines New York.

**A Cultural Melting Pot**

New York's diversity is its greatest strength. The city celebrates all cultures, cuisines, and traditions, creating a rich tapestry of human experience. This blend of old and new, tradition and innovation, makes New York truly one of a kind.

In the end, New York remains a symbol of hope and possibility—a place where all dreams can find their beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short prose poem describing a surreal dream about marching through a ruined New York with the poet Mayakovsky, who discusses poetry as you walk.
counterfactuals.output:
**Marching with Mayakovsky Through the Ruins**

We came down Broadway at the hour when the sky forgets its color, and Mayakovsky walked beside me with his coat like a torn flag, his jaw a monument to some demolished certainty. The skyscrapers had knelt. Their steel ribs showed through like the bones of whales beached on an avenue of ash.

*Poetry*, he said, *is not a lullaby. It is a hammer left out in the rain.* And where his boots struck the pavement, small alphabets scattered—vowels rolling into the gutters, consonants sharp as broken glass.

We passed a traffic light still blinking its dead instructions to no one. He laughed, a sound like a train entering a tunnel. *They wanted my verses smooth. I gave them a staircase with the steps removed.*

Overhead, the pigeons had become paper, unfolding into manifestos as they flew. I tried to read them but the wind was faster than my eyes.

*You are too quiet*, he told me. *A poem must shout even when it whispers. Even the dust here is shouting—listen.* And I listened, and the ruins were full of a low articulate roar, the city reciting itself backward into rubble.

At the harbor the water stood upright, a green wall holding back the drowned. Mayakovsky stopped. He looked enormous against it, a man arguing with the ocean. *This*, he said, *is the last line. Everything before it was only clearing the throat.*

Then he stepped into the water as into a doorway, and the wall closed over him without a ripple, and I woke with salt on my lips and a hammer-weight in my chest, still marching, still marching.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dreamlike piece of flash fiction in which the narrator confesses a dream and encounters Mayakovsky, blending Soviet imagery with reflections on how poems work from the inside.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Machinist of Vowels**

I confess: last night I dreamed in red, and the red was a language.

I was walking through a city built entirely of unfinished sentences—girders of syntax rising into a sky the color of a Party banner left too long in rain. The scaffolding hummed. Somewhere a loudspeaker recited the weather in iambs, and I understood that here the weather was always a metaphor for something we were not permitted to name directly.

Mayakovsky found me at the base of a statue that was still arguing with its own pedestal.

He was enormous, of course—all jaw and shoulder, a man built like a slogan. He wore his voice the way other men wear coats. When he spoke, pigeons rearranged themselves into exclamation points.

"You want to know how it works," he said. Not a question. He had the manner of someone who'd already read your future in the newspaper.

"How what works?"

"The engine." He knocked on my sternum with one knuckle, and it rang hollow, industrial. "A poem is not a mirror, comrade. A mirror only agrees with you. A poem is a *turbine*." He gestured at the humming girders. "You force meaning through the narrow place until it screams. That scream—that pressure—that is the line break. You think the white space is silence?" He laughed, and the pavement cracked into stanzas. "The white space is where the machine catches its breath before it lifts the next ton of the world."

I told him I'd always thought poems were feeling.

"Feeling!" He spat, and where it landed a small flower of enjambment grew. "Feeling is only the coal. Anyone can burn. The question is the *furnace*—how you build the chamber so the burning does work, moves the piston, drives the wheel. A hundred poets are on fire this minute. They warm no one. They lack a *mechanism*."

Above us the loudspeaker changed its recitation. It was reading his own name back to him, and I saw him flinch—the great machine of him developing, for one instant, a flaw in the casting.

"They will make me into a boulevard," he said quietly. "A subway station. That is what a country does with a poet it could not answer. It embalms the pressure. It puts the turbine in a glass case and calls it *heritage*." He looked at me with something like tenderness, which on his architecture looked like structural fatigue. "Do you understand? From the *outside* a poem is a monument. Only from the inside is it still spinning. You must always read from inside the machine. You must climb in among the moving parts and let them take a finger if they want one."

I asked what happens to the reader in there.

"You are pushed through the narrow place," he said. "Same as the meaning. You come out smaller and truer and screaming a little. That scream—" he tapped my chest again, and this time it rang like a bell, like a bell that had decided to become a fist—"that scream is the poem completing itself in you. The poem is not finished on the page. The page is only the blueprint. *You* are the factory floor."

The city was dissolving now, the unfinished sentences finishing themselves badly, the way dreams edit toward morning. Mayakovsky was becoming translucent, becoming boulevard, becoming the cold weight of a collected edition on a shelf.

"Wait," I said. "How do I know if mine works? My poems?"

He was almost gone—just jaw now, just the memory of enormous shoulders, just a voice wearing the last of its coat.

"Put your ear to it," he said, "the way you'd listen to a rail for the coming train. If you hear nothing, it is a decoration. If you feel the tremor before you hear the sound—"

The loudspeaker cut him off with a hymn to tractor output.

I woke with my hand on my sternum, listening. And I confess: somewhere far down the line, under all that red, something enormous was still coming, and it had not yet decided whether to stop for me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person surrealist vignette that begins by admitting it was just a dream, set on the bleak industrial outskirts of a city, featuring a conversation with a famous poet about the nature of writing poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Foundry District

It was just a dream, I know that now, the way you know things after the fact—retroactively, like a debt.

I was walking the outskirts where the city gives up on itself. Warehouses with their windows punched out. A canal the color of an old nickel. Smokestacks that had forgotten how to smoke, standing like the fingers of a hand pushed up through the earth by someone drowning underneath it.

Federico García Lorca was sitting on an overturned oil drum, and I was not surprised. In dreams the dead keep the appointments the living cancel.

"You've come the wrong way," he said. He was cleaning something under his nails with a splinter of moonlight. "Everyone comes the wrong way. That's the only way to arrive."

I asked him how to write a poem. I had traveled a long way to ask this, though the way had been circular and I had passed the same dead factory four times.

He laughed, and pigeons lifted off a girder in a gray applause.

"You don't write it," he said. "You dig a well and wait to hear if anything answers. Sometimes it is water. Sometimes it is a voice complaining that you've disturbed its sleep. Sometimes"—he held up the drum's rusted lid like a mirror—"it is only your own face, gone stupid with wanting."

The canal behind us began, very quietly, to run backward.

"But the *technique*," I insisted, because I was young in the dream, and the young want a ladder to a place best reached by falling.

"Technique." He said the word the way you'd handle a beautiful knife that had cut you before. "Technique is the horse. The poem is the country the horse refuses to enter. You must make the horse believe you are going somewhere else. You must lie to the horse. You must lie to yourself in the same breath, and both of you must be surprised when you arrive."

A bell was ringing somewhere in the shipping yards, though there was no one to ring it, and no ship, and no faith.

"The duende lives here," he said, gesturing at the ruin, the ash-lots, the puddles skinned with oil making rainbows out of poison. "Not in your gardens. Not in your libraries with their green lamps. Here. Where the machines died and left their loneliness lying around like tools. A poem must smell a little of this place. If it smells only of the desk, throw it in the canal."

I looked and the canal was full of paper, thousands of white pages turning slowly, going soft, becoming the color of the water, becoming the water.

"Are those poems?" I asked.

"Those are the ones that were true," he said. "The false ones we keep. The false ones win prizes. Come."

But when I turned to follow, he was already a smokestack, or had always been one, and the splinter of moon he'd held was rising back into a sky the color of a struck match, and I understood I was being asked to leave the way you're asked by a landlord who has changed the locks—politely, and without appeal.

I woke with rust on my hands.

I have not been able to wash it off. I am not entirely sure I have tried.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece in the style of John Ashbery or a New York School poet: a prose poem where the speaker walks in a column of downtrodden men, talks with Mayakovsky about being "inside the poem," and the poem ends when the poet leaves.
counterfactuals.output:
The Column

We were walking, and the walking was a kind of weather. Overcoats the color of unwashed windows, and each man carrying the small brown parcel of himself down the avenue that had forgotten its own name. I did not choose this line; it accreted around me the way frost decides a fence.

Mayakovsky was there, of course, because he is always somewhere just ahead, turning back his enormous face like a searchlight that has grown tired of the harbor. "You understand," he said, and the sidewalk repeated it, "that we are inside the poem now." I asked him whether that meant we could not leave, and he laughed the way a bridge laughs, all at once and made of iron. "It means the leaving is also written. It means your feet are a stanza and you are wearing them out."

The other men said nothing. That is the condition of being downtrodden: the speech has been taken out of you and placed in a display case at the front of the procession, where you may look at it but not touch. Still, I felt an obscure gladness, the way one does at the exact moment a thing becomes irretrievable. To be *inside*—yes. The walls were made of the same gray light that was making us, and the ceiling, when I looked up, was simply more of us, walking on the underside, going the other way.

"Say something true," Mayakovsky demanded, "before the margins close." But I could think only of how the coffee had tasted that morning, burnt and generous, and of a woman on a staircase in nineteen-something who had turned to see if I was following. These are not truths. They are the small change of truth, the coins you keep because the amount is too small to bank and too heavy to throw away.

He seemed satisfied. He always is, in the end; his dissatisfaction is a stage he keeps for the balconies. We passed a fountain that had been drained for the season, and the men bent, one by one, to drink from it anyway, out of habit, out of the memory of water. This, I thought, is what a poem is: the gesture that outlasts its reason. The mouth going down to the dry stone.

And then—I want to be accurate about this—he simply was not there. Not a departure so much as a subtraction. The searchlight face swung once toward Petersburg, toward the year that took him, and then the space where he had been filled quietly with more overcoat, more gray, more Tuesday. The men closed over the gap without malice. The column went on.

That is when I knew it was ending, because the poet had gone, and the poet was the one thing the poem could not survive. The light thinned to the width of a held breath. Somewhere a door I could not see was being politely opened. I kept walking, downtrodden and enormous, wearing out my only stanza, until the sentence I was standing in

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imaginative, melancholic dream narrative involving Vladimir Mayakovsky, muddy paths, proletarian rags, and a meditation on how large poems have "more room inside."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Poem

I dreamt of Mayakovsky walking ahead of me, his enormous shoulders cutting through a fog the color of dishwater. The path beneath us was mud—not the honest mud of fields but the churned, exhausted mud of a city that had been marched over too many times. My boots pulled at it with each step, that wet sucking sound like the earth asking a question it already knew the answer to.

He wore rags. This surprised me, because in photographs he is always so magnificent, so architectural in his coat. But here he wore the proletarian's uniform of frayed wool and patched elbows, and somehow it suited him better—as though the poet had finally dressed in the material of the people he had shouted himself hoarse for.

"You're following me," he said without turning. His voice was the low register of a foghorn.

"I don't know the way."

"Nobody does. That's why we build the long poems." He stopped and swept his arm across the grey nothing. "A short poem is a room you rent. You come, you weep, you leave before the landlord knocks. But a long poem—" he pressed his fist to his chest, "—a long poem you can *live* in. It has more room inside. Corridors. Attics where you hide the things you couldn't say."

We walked on. The mud deepened. I understood, in the strange grammar of dreams, that we were walking *into* one of his poems, that the fog was stanzas and the path was a single unspooling line.

"In here," he said, "there is room for the revolution *and* the woman who wouldn't love me. Room for the placards and the private grief. You cannot fit a whole man in a sonnet. You fold him, you break his knees to make him fit." He laughed, but it was the saddest sound I had ever heard—a laugh that had been standing in the rain a long time.

I looked at his rags and understood they were also words. Everything here was made of language worn thin by use. The patches were revisions. The frayed cuffs were lines he had crossed out and could not quite abandon.

"Are you happy in here?" I asked.

He considered this for a long time, the way the enormous consider small questions.

"There is *room* to be happy," he said finally. "That is not the same. But it is more than the sonnets give. In the small forms you must decide. In the large ones you may simply—continue. You keep walking, and the poem keeps making more path in front of your boots." He gestured at the mud unrolling into fog. "See? It has not ended. It will not end while I keep speaking."

And I understood then why he built them so vast, those cathedrals of shouting and tenderness. Not from vanity. From fear. A long poem is a place where the poet does not yet have to stop. Where the last line, the final rhyme, the small black period that waits for every man—all of it stays somewhere ahead, dissolved in fog, postponed by the sheer generous acreage of the thing.

"Keep walking with me," he said, and it was almost a plea from a man who was usually all command. "As long as we walk, the poem has more room. As long as there is room, I don't have to reach the end."

So we walked. The mud pulled at our boots. The fog gave up more path, and more, and more.

I woke before we stopped. I like to think they never did.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
